svg.title: Stacking against multi-chassis aggregation across six dimensions, ending with where each one belongs
svg.desc: A six row comparison of stacking and multi-chassis aggregation. Stacking has a single control plane and one configuration, upgrades the whole stack together, shares fate across every member, and depends on the stack cable as a single point. Multi-chassis aggregation keeps two control planes that must be kept consistent, upgrades one member at a time, keeps failure domains independent, and depends on the peer link and keepalive being physically separate. A note recommends stacking for access layers and clustering for core and distribution, and lists the three single points that come with stacking.
svg.text: Stacking and clustering both remove blocked ports; they differ in what they make inseparable
One control plane is convenient at the access layer and dangerous under a core
DIMENSION
STACKING · STACKWISE, VSS
CLUSTERING · vPC, MLAG
Control plane
one, with one configuration file
two, which must be kept in step by discipline
Forwarding
all uplinks forward, no STP blocking
all uplinks forward, no STP blocking
Software upgrade
every member reboots together
one member at a time, traffic keeps flowing
Failure domain
shared fate: one bug, one config error, all members
independent, at the cost of consistency drift
The single point
the stacking cable: broken, and the stack splits
peer link and keepalive: separated, or one post
Where it belongs
access layer, dense port counts, small sites
core, distribution, data centre leaf pairs
STACKING'S THREE SINGLE POINTS
1. the stack cable or ring — one bad member can break the stack
2. the master election — a master failure restarts the control plane
3. the shared configuration — one typo reaches every port at once
CLUSTERING'S THREE DEBTS
1. two configurations that must agree, checked by nobody
2. a peer link that carries all cross traffic and all failures
3. a split brain mode that needs an external detector
The rule of thumb that survives contact with operations: stack where a single management plane saves more than a shared failure costs; cluster where an upgrade window matters.
Access closets have neither rolling upgrades nor long-running sessions worth protecting, and they have forty ports nobody wants to configure twice.
A core has both: it has sessions, it has a maintenance window, and it has no appetite for a master election at two in the morning.
Both are legitimate; what is not legitimate is choosing one and claiming it has no cost.
